chapter_title: Setting Up the Player and Movement

screens.title: Setting Up the Player and Movement
screens.subtitle: Create a script-driven player with collision-aware movement using CharacterBody2D

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a basic, responsive 2D player using Godot's CharacterBody2D. We'll focus on three practical pieces: creating a player scene with a Sprite2D and a CollisionShape2D so collisions are reliable, writing physics-tied movement inside _physics_process so behavior is frame-rate stable, and using move_and_slide to ensure the player collides and slides along surfaces smoothly. You will see how gravity, horizontal control, and jumping fit together into a single velocity vector so that all motion is consistent. This matters because a character that bypasses Godot's collision methods can pass through walls or behave unpredictably on different machines. As an example, we will use a placeholder sprite and a rectangle collision shape, then attach a short GDScript that applies gravity, reads input via the Input singleton, and calls move_and_slide. A common misconception is that directly changing position or using the non-physics process is adequate for collision-aware movement; we'll clarify why that leads to tunneling or missed collisions. By the end of this chapter you will have a test scene with a StaticBody2D floor and an instanced Player that moves left and right, falls under gravity, and jumps only when on the floor. Consider how these fundamentals let you tune speed, jump feel, and collision bounds for a polished platformer.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use CharacterBody2D + CollisionShape2D, update motion in _physics_process, and call move_and_slide for collision-aware, script-driven player movement.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to assemble a player scene with a CharacterBody2D root, a Sprite2D, and an accurate CollisionShape2D so collisions feel natural. You will implement physics-aware movement using _physics_process that keeps behavior consistent across frame rates. You will read player input through Godot's Input singleton to drive horizontal motion and jumping. Finally, you will apply move_and_slide to perform collision-aware movement and avoid common errors such as modifying position directly or updating movement in the wrong callback. For example, you will create a Player. gd script that applies gravity to a velocity vector, uses action strengths for left/right movement, uses move_toward to decelerate smoothly, and calls move_and_slide to let Godot resolve collisions. Each of these objectives builds toward a testable milestone: a player that moves and collides correctly on a StaticBody2D floor. We'll also point out common pitfalls and how to test shape alignment so your player doesn’t get stuck on edges.

screens.title: What is CharacterBody2D?
screens.subtitle: A script-driven body that still participates in collisions

narration.text: CharacterBody2D is a specialized node designed for characters that you control primarily by script. Unlike physics-driven rigid bodies, a CharacterBody2D gives you direct control over velocity and movement while still using Godot's collision detection system. In practice, that means you write the rules for how the character moves and Godot helps with collision resolution when you use movement helpers like move_and_slide. A concrete example: you control the player's horizontal speed and jump velocity in script, and call move_and_slide so the engine detects floors and walls and slides the player appropriately. A common misconception is to treat CharacterBody2D exactly like a StaticBody2D or to directly set position; while CharacterBody2D is script-controlled, it is still a physics body and needs its movement methods to cooperate with collision responses. Another contrast is with RigidBody2D, which reacts to applied forces and the physics engine; that is ideal for objects governed by physics, not player-controlled characters where precise input responsiveness matters. Key practical details include that CharacterBody2D provides a velocity vector property you update and functions such as is_on_floor to check contact. Think of CharacterBody2D as a cooperative partner: you script behavior, and the engine enforces collisions and sliding when you hand movement to it. How would you adjust your speed or jump to feel more responsive once collisions are correct?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CharacterBody2D is a controlled physics body: script-driven motion plus engine collision resolution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is CharacterBody2D?
CharacterBody2D
A node for characters that are primarily controlled by code but need collision detection.
Core properties
  • Provides a velocity Vector2 that your code updates each physics frame.
  • Offers helpers like is_on_floor to check contact points.
  • Works with move_and_slide so collisions are resolved by the engine.
Misconception
Treating it like a StaticBody2D or changing position manually defeats collision handling and causes tunneling.
Key Takeaway

Choose CharacterBody2D for precise script-driven player motion while retaining engine collision resolution.

Analogy
Think of CharacterBody2D as a car you drive manually; the physics engine provides the road and collision rules so you can't drive through walls if you steer into them while using the proper controls.
Quick contrast
RigidBody2D
Physics-driven, reacts to forces and impulses.
CharacterBody2D
Script-driven motion with engine collision helpers.
Code hint
Use a velocity Vector2 and call move_and_slide() from _physics_process to move a CharacterBody2D.

screens.title: Scene Setup: Player Node and Children
screens.subtitle: Create a CharacterBody2D with Sprite2D and CollisionShape2D

narration.text: Building the player scene is the first hands-on step. Begin by creating a new 2D scene and change the root node to CharacterBody2D. Name it Player so it’s clear in the tree. Next add two child nodes: Sprite2D for visuals and CollisionShape2D to define the physical bounds. For the Sprite2D use any placeholder texture such as the default icon if you don’t yet have art. For CollisionShape2D choose a simple RectangleShape2D or CapsuleShape2D and resize it in the editor until it matches the visible sprite. Proper alignment is essential: if the collision shape is too small you may see the player clip into floors; if it’s offset the floor checks like is_on_floor can misbehave. After you add nodes, attach a new GDScript to the Player node named Player. gd. This script will hold exported variables such as speed, jump_velocity, and gravity so you can tweak them without changing code. A common pitfall is forgetting to add the CollisionShape2D or leaving it disabled—this makes the character a ghost without collisions. Another mistake is using overly complex shapes early; start simple and iterate. Verify your setup by running the scene with a StaticBody2D floor in the main scene and confirming the collision shape overlaps the floor as expected. This process yields a clean player scene ready for movement logic.

keyIdea.title: Scene pattern
keyIdea.text: Player scene = CharacterBody2D root + Sprite2D visual + CollisionShape2D collision; attach Player.gd to control motion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Scene Setup
Step-by-step
  1. Create a new 2D scene and change the root to CharacterBody2D. Rename it Player.
  2. Add Sprite2D as a child. Load a placeholder texture such as icon.svg.
  3. Add CollisionShape2D as a child. Assign RectangleShape2D or CapsuleShape2D and resize to fit the sprite.
  4. Attach a script Player.gd to the Player node and export variables for tuning.
  5. Place a StaticBody2D floor in the main scene to test collisions.
Example
Use RectangleShape2D sized to the sprite bounds; toggle shape visibility while running to check alignment.
Common Pitfalls
  • Forgetting CollisionShape2D or leaving it disabled—player will not collide.
  • Misaligned shape causing floor checks to fail or the player to get stuck on edges.
  • Using overly complex collision shapes initially; keep shapes simple.
Key Takeaway

Set up a clear player scene structure and confirm collision shape alignment before coding movement logic.

screens.title: _physics_process(delta)
screens.subtitle: Why physics updates belong in the fixed loop

narration.text: _physics_process runs on the physics tick and is the right place for movement and collision logic. Physics frames run at a fixed rate, which prevents movement from varying with frame rate. When you update forces, velocities, or call movement helpers, put that code inside _physics_process so the physics engine receives consistent inputs. For example, applying gravity every physics frame as velocity. y += gravity * delta keeps acceleration consistent across different machines. A common mistake is to update motion inside _process, the variable-rate rendering loop. Doing so can cause inconsistent collision checks, tunneling at high frame rates, or jerky motion at low frame rates. Another subtle point is that delta inside _physics_process is the physics delta and aligns with collision resolution timing; this makes checks like is_on_floor more reliable. When you call move_and_slide from _physics_process you hand the engine a velocity that matches the current physics tick, letting collisions be resolved immediately. To test this, compare behavior with the same code placed in _process; you will notice different timing and unreliable floor detection. Remember: use _physics_process for anything that affects physics or collision behavior.

keyIdea.title: Physics loop
keyIdea.text: Put gravity, velocity updates, and move_and_slide calls inside _physics_process for consistent, frame-rate-independent physics.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › _physics_process(delta)
Fixed-rate updates for physics
Use this callback to update velocity and call movement functions so collisions are predictable.
  • Physics frames run at a fixed tick; multiply accelerations by delta for frame-rate independence.
  • is_on_floor checks are most reliable when performed in the physics loop.
  • move_and_slide should be called inside _physics_process to align movement with collision resolution.
Misconception check
Do not use _process for physics updates; its variable timing can cause missed collisions and inconsistent movement feel.
Code pattern
func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
  # Apply gravity and movement here
  velocity.y += gravity * delta
  handle_input()
  move_and_slide()
Pro tip

Treat _physics_process as the single source of truth for movement logic; keep visuals and animation playback in _process if needed.

screens.title: Velocity and Coordinate System
screens.subtitle: How velocity Vector2 models motion and why Y is inverted

narration.text: In Godot 2D, movement is expressed through a velocity Vector2 that contains x and y components. The x component controls horizontal speed and direction; positive x moves right and negative x moves left. The y component controls vertical motion, but remember the coordinate system uses positive Y downwards, so an upward jump sets velocity. y to a negative value. In player scripts you typically adjust velocity. x for left and right input and change velocity. y when applying gravity or a jump impulse. Because velocity represents pixels per second, multiplying accelerations by delta keeps motion consistent across different frame rates and physics ticks. An example: when the player jumps you set velocity. y to jump_velocity, often a negative number like -250. As the physics loop runs, gravity adds to velocity. y every physics frame, bringing the player back down. Misreading Y direction is a frequent source of bugs: trying to set a positive jump value pushes the player downward instead of up. Another practical note is to avoid mixing direct position changes with velocity updates; consistently using velocity and movement helpers maintains collision behavior. In short, treat velocity as your single authoritative representation of motion and think in screen coordinates where down is positive.

keyIdea.title: Velocity vector
keyIdea.text: Use velocity.x for horizontal motion and velocity.y for vertical motion; negative Y moves up because Y increases downward.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Velocity and Coordinates
Velocity Vector2
x controls horizontal speed; y controls vertical speed and follows screen coordinates where down is positive.
  • Set velocity.x from input strengths for left/right movement.
  • Apply gravity to velocity.y every physics frame: velocity.y += gravity * delta.
  • Set velocity.y to a negative jump_velocity to move upward on jump.
Misconception
Assuming positive Y is up will invert jump and gravity behavior—use negative jump_velocity to go up.
Quick example
# conceptual snippet
var velocity = Vector2.ZERO
# apply gravity
velocity.y += gravity * delta
# jump
if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and is_on_floor():
  velocity.y = jump_velocity
# horizontal
velocity.x = direction_x * speed
move_and_slide()
Key Takeaway

Treat velocity as pixels-per-second; remember negative y moves the player upward.

screens.title: Using the Input Singleton
screens.subtitle: Read actions and strengths for flexible controls

narration.text: Godot's Input singleton provides a consistent way to query player controls. Use Input. is_action_pressed or Input. get_action_strength to read mapped actions such as ui_right, ui_left, and ui_accept. The advantage of actions is that users can remap keys in Project Settings -> Input Map without you changing code. For horizontal movement a common pattern is to compute direction_x as Input. get_action_strength("ui_right") - Input. get_action_strength("ui_left"), resulting in -1, 0, or 1 for keyboard input and fractional values for gamepad axes. For jumping use Input. is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") so you trigger a single impulse rather than continuous jumps while holding the button. One practical example: when direction_x is non-zero set velocity. x = direction_x * speed; when it’s zero call move_toward to decelerate smoothly. A frequent mistake is to poll raw keys instead of mapped actions, which prevents easy remapping and gamepad support. Also avoid reading input in _physics_process and simultaneously using different input methods in separate places—centralize input reading so behavior stays predictable. In testing, check keyboard and gamepad behaviors to ensure action strengths produce the expected movement numbers. Using the Input Singleton means use input.get_action_strength and is_action_just_pressed for remappable, consistent control input across devices.. In practical terms, read actions and strengths for flexible controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Input pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Input.get_action_strength and is_action_just_pressed for remappable, consistent control input across devices.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Input Singleton
Read mapped actions
Action strengths support keyboard and gamepad and allow remapping in Project Settings.
  • Use get_action_strength("ui_right") - get_action_strength("ui_left") for horizontal direction.
  • Use is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") for single-tap jump triggers.
  • Keep input reads in _physics_process for consistent reaction to physics ticks.
Pro tip
Favor action names rather than hard-coded keys so players can remap controls easily and support gamepads naturally.
Input example
var direction_x = Input.get_action_strength("ui_right") - Input.get_action_strength("ui_left")
if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and is_on_floor():
  velocity.y = jump_velocity
if direction_x:
  velocity.x = direction_x * speed
Common mistake

Polling raw key events rather than actions makes remapping and gamepad input harder to support later.

narration.text: Gravity is a constant downward acceleration you apply to the player's vertical velocity each physics frame. In practice you declare an exported gravity variable and then add gravity * delta to velocity. y each call to _physics_process. Multiplying by delta is essential because physics ticks represent a time step; without delta, gravity would scale with frame-rate and the player would fall faster on machines with higher tick rates. A simple pattern is to check if the player is not on the floor before applying gravity so you don't keep accumulating downward speed once grounded. In code: if not is_on_floor(): velocity. y += gravity * delta. When the player jumps, you directly set velocity. y to jump_velocity, a negative number, and subsequent physics ticks will start adding gravity again until the player lands. A frequent oversight is applying gravity without delta or applying it while also changing position manually; both lead to inconsistent falling and collision results. Tuning gravity and jump_velocity together gives you the desired feel; stronger gravity shortens airtime, while a larger negative jump_velocity makes a higher initial jump. Test combinations with the StaticBody2D floor until the arc feels right.

keyIdea.title: Gravity rule
keyIdea.text: Apply gravity each physics frame as velocity.y += gravity * delta and only while the player is airborne.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Applying Gravity
Gravity pattern
Apply gravity as acceleration multiplied by delta for consistent falling behavior.
  • Only apply gravity if the character is airborne to prevent buildup while grounded.
  • Multiply gravity by delta to keep behavior independent from frame rate.
  • Tune gravity and jump velocity together for desired hang time and responsiveness.
Example
velocity.y += gravity * delta when not is_on_floor(); set velocity.y = jump_velocity to jump upward.
Tuning guide
If your jumps feel floaty, increase gravity or lower jump_velocity. If jumps feel too short, decrease gravity or increase negative jump_velocity.
Key Takeaway

Gravity is an acceleration applied each physics frame; always multiply by delta and tune alongside jump_velocity.

screens.title: Jump Handling and Floor Checks
screens.subtitle: Use is_on_floor and just-pressed input for reliable jumps

narration.text: Jumping reliably requires two elements: a check that the player is grounded and a one-shot input trigger. Use is_on_floor to determine whether the character is standing on a surface; only allow jumps when this returns true. For input, prefer Input. is_action_just_pressed so holding the jump button doesn't continually reapply jump velocity. In practice, in _physics_process you might write: if Input. is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and is_on_floor(): velocity. y = jump_velocity. This sets an upward impulse in velocity. y and then subsequent physics frames add gravity back onto that velocity so the arc forms naturally. A common error is using is_action_pressed instead of is_action_just_pressed; that can cause repeated jump impulses if the condition allows it. Another is misaligning the CollisionShape2D so is_on_floor returns false even when the sprite visually touches the ground; verify the shape and experiment with a slightly larger or lower collision shape if needed. For slopes and small ledges, move_and_slide handles sliding, but you may need extra checks for step snapping later. Start with a simple grounded check and single-press jump to get reliable, predictable results. Jump Handling and Floor Checks means use is_on_floor to gate jumps and is_action_just_pressed to trigger a single jump impulse into velocity.y.. In practical terms, use is_on_floor and just-pressed input for reliable jumps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Jump rule
keyIdea.text: Use is_on_floor to gate jumps and is_action_just_pressed to trigger a single jump impulse into velocity.y.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Jump Handling
Grounded jump pattern
Only allow a jump when the engine reports the body is on the floor and the jump action is just pressed.
  • Check is_on_floor to ensure the player is grounded.
  • Use Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") to apply a single jump impulse.
  • Set velocity.y = jump_velocity, then gravity will act on future frames.
Debug tip
Toggle CollisionShape2D visibility to confirm the collision bottom overlaps the floor and that is_on_floor returns true when expected.
Jump snippet
if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and is_on_floor():
  velocity.y = jump_velocity
Key Takeaway

Gate jumps with a floor check and trigger with a just-pressed action to avoid repeated impulses.

screens.title: Player.gd — Full Example
screens.subtitle: A minimal, correct script for movement, gravity, and jumping

narration.text: Let's walk through a compact Player. gd that demonstrates the complete pattern. The script extends CharacterBody2D and exports three tuning variables: speed, jump_velocity, and gravity. Inside _physics_process we apply gravity to velocity. y only when not on the floor, check for a just-pressed jump to set velocity. y to jump_velocity, read horizontal input via get_action_strength and update velocity. x accordingly, and use move_toward to decelerate when there's no input. Finally, move_and_slide hands the velocity to the engine for collision-aware movement. This pattern centralizes motion in a single velocity variable and relies on engine helpers for collision. A concrete example is the script provided in the chapter; when you attach it to the Player node and instance the Player in a scene with a StaticBody2D floor, moving left and right and jumping should work immediately. A common area for improvement is clamping terminal velocity or adding air control tweaks, but the core loop demonstrates safe, frame-rate-independent movement and collision handling. After you paste the script, test it and adjust exported parameters to dial in the feel. Player.gd — Full Example means a single player.gd updates velocity in _physics_process, reads input, applies gravity, and calls move_and_slide.. In practical terms, a minimal, correct script for movement, gravity, and jumping. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: A single Player.gd updates velocity in _physics_process, reads input, applies gravity, and calls move_and_slide.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Player.gd Example
Full GDScript (copy into Player.gd)
# Player.gd
extends CharacterBody2D

@export var speed: float = 100.0
@export var jump_velocity: float = -250.0 # Negative for upwards movement
@export var gravity: float = 400.0

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
    # Apply gravity
    if not is_on_floor():
        velocity.y += gravity * delta

    # Handle jump input
    if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept") and is_on_floor():
        velocity.y = jump_velocity

    # Get horizontal input
    var direction_x = Input.get_action_strength("ui_right") - Input.get_action_strength("ui_left")
    if direction_x:
        velocity.x = direction_x * speed
    else:
        velocity.x = move_toward(velocity.x, 0, speed * delta) # Smooth stop

    # Move the character
    move_and_slide()
Explanation
  • Exported variables make tuning easier in the Inspector without editing code.
  • Gravity is applied when airborne and multiplied by delta for frame-rate safety.
  • Direction uses action strengths to support keyboard and gamepad input.
  • move_toward creates a smooth deceleration instead of instant stopping.
Key Takeaway

This script is a minimal, robust starting point; export and test values to achieve your desired game feel.

narration.text: Smooth horizontal control contributes significantly to how a player 'feels'. Rather than snapping velocity. x to zero when input stops, use move_toward to gradually reduce horizontal speed. move_toward(velocity. x, 0, speed * delta) reduces velocity. x toward zero at a rate proportional to speed and delta, producing a natural deceleration. When directional input exists, set velocity. x directly to direction_x * speed so the character responds immediately to control; when input is absent, call move_toward to slow the character. This also helps when transitioning to animations because you can compute movement speed from velocity. x and smoothly blend animation states. A common issue is setting velocity. x = 0 instantly, which makes movement feel stiff and cuts off momentum. Another nuance is that you may want reduced control in air: apply a smaller max speed or slower move_toward when not is_on_floor to produce more realistic airborne movement. Test combinations of speed and deceleration to find a sweet spot: fast response with gentle stopping tends to feel polished for platformers. Smooth Horizontal Movement and Stopping means use move_toward to decelerate velocity.x toward zero so stops feel natural instead of abrupt.. In practical terms, use move_toward to decelerate naturally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Smooth stopping
keyIdea.text: Use move_toward to decelerate velocity.x toward zero so stops feel natural instead of abrupt.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Smooth Horizontal Movement
Instant vs Smooth
Avoid snapping velocity.x to zero. Use move_toward for natural deceleration and better animation blending.
  • When input exists: velocity.x = direction_x * speed for immediate response.
  • When no input: velocity.x = move_toward(velocity.x, 0, speed * delta) for smooth stopping.
  • Consider reduced horizontal control in air by scaling speed when not is_on_floor.
Practical tip
Tune the third argument of move_toward to control how quickly the player slows—higher values stop faster, lower values give glide.
Snippet
if direction_x:
  velocity.x = direction_x * speed
else:
  velocity.x = move_toward(velocity.x, 0, speed * delta)
Key Takeaway

Smooth deceleration improves feel and helps animation timing; avoid abrupt stops unless the game requires them.

screens.title: move_and_slide() and Collision Resolution
screens.subtitle: Let Godot handle sliding and contact resolution

narration.text: move_and_slide is the method that transfers your velocity to the physics engine and asks it to move the body while resolving collisions. When you call move_and_slide() on a CharacterBody2D, Godot attempts to move the body according to the velocity and automatically adjusts movement if collisions occur, sliding the body along surfaces instead of abruptly stopping. This creates smooth behavior on walls and slopes. The method also updates internal contact information so functions like is_on_floor can work. A common mistake is to move the node by changing position or using translate; those bypass collision resolution and lead to objects passing through geometry. Another practical point is that move_and_slide can take additional parameters for floor-normal or up direction if you later add slope logic; but the default behavior is sufficient for most platformers. For realistic collision response, ensure the CollisionShape2D is positioned so that the engine can detect contact at the expected points. When testing, walk the player into walls and confirm the character slides rather than jittering or tunneling. Rely on move_and_slide as your collision-savvy movement call and avoid manual position manipulation for physics bodies.

keyIdea.title: move_and_slide
keyIdea.text: Call move_and_slide to hand velocity to the engine so collisions and sliding are resolved automatically.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › move_and_slide()
Collision-aware movement
Use move_and_slide to let Godot resolve collisions, sliding along surfaces rather than stopping abruptly.
  • move_and_slide takes your velocity and moves the body with collision resolution.
  • It enables reliable contact checks such as is_on_floor after the move.
  • Avoid changing position directly for bodies that must collide.
Behavior check

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, use CharacterBody2D for script-driven characters so you can control motion while keeping collision detection. Second, build the Player scene with a Sprite2D for visuals and a CollisionShape2D sized to match the sprite; misaligned shapes cause most collision bugs.
